query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small, optimized concentration of reactive elements (specifically Y and Hf) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve its stability under cyclic high-temperature and corrosive conditions by promoting the formation of stable, fine precipitates at grain boundaries and more adherent, protective oxide scales.
generation.material_initial_state: The base AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring a uniform, fine lamellar structure produced by conventional processing.
generation.intervention: Microalloying the alloy with trace additions of Y and Hf.
generation.conditions: Exposure to extreme temperature fluctuations (e.g., around 900 °C with thermal cycling), long-term mechanical loading including room-temperature creep, and corrosive environments such as those containing molten salts (75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl).
generation.structural_mediator: The reactive dopants promote nucleation of an Al-rich L12 phase and other nanoscale precipitates at the grain boundaries, leading to reduced grain boundary mobility and enhanced adherence of the protective oxide scales.
generation.mechanism: Y and Hf segregate to grain boundaries during thermal exposure, which impedes grain coarsening and retards dislocation motion. In parallel, these dopants improve the formation and adhesion of stable oxide scales that resist spallation, thereby mitigating high-temperature corrosion and creep phenomena.
generation.predicted_outcome: Doped alloys will exhibit reduced grain coarsening under thermal cycling, lower creep rates under long-term mechanical loading, and enhanced resistance to hot corrosion (e.g., reduced oxide scale spallation) compared with the base alloy, thereby achieving a better strength–ductility balance under industrially relevant conditions.
generation.baseline: The base AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy without microalloying shows relatively faster grain growth under heat treatment, a higher susceptibility to creep deformation, and less robust oxide scale formation, resulting in suboptimal performance under extreme temperature and corrosive conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected under high-temperature conditions (around 900 °C) with thermal cycling and in environments with corrosive salt deposits. The improvements depend on the dopant levels being optimized; excessive or insufficient additions could disrupt phase equilibrium or fail to confer the desired benefits.
generation.uncertainty: Precise dopant concentrations and long-term behavior under realistic service conditions remain to be validated. The interplay between improved oxide scale adhesion and potential increases in spallation (as noted in some coating studies) must be carefully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one using the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and one with the addition of optimized trace amounts of Y and Hf. Subject both sets to cyclic high-temperature treatment at 900 °C in the presence of a corrosive salt mixture (75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl) and conduct long-term mechanical loading tests to assess creep behavior. Characterize the microstructure evolution (grain size and precipitate formation) via SEM/TEM and evaluate corrosion resistance using surface spallation analysis.
measurements: Grain size and distribution of nanoscale precipitates (via TEM/SEM)
Oxide scale adherence and percentage of spallation areas
Creep rate under a constant load
Tensile strength and ductility before and after thermal/corrosive exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-Hf doped samples do not show statistically significant improvements in creep resistance (i.e., lower creep rates), grain coarsening control, and lower oxide scale spallation compared to the baseline alloy under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. In this study, the Y and Hf co-doping did not change the microstructure morphology and phase structure of the coatings but did improve the thermal stability and resistance of the hot corrosion oxide scale spallation, providing a certain amount of data and theoretical support for the application of EHEA coat

## Abstract
Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs.
